title: How Childhood Vaccines Work
hook: Vaccines train a child's immune system to recognize a disease in advance, so it can fight off the real thing — and they're scheduled to protect kids when they're most vulnerable.
key_points: A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless piece or weakened form of a germ, building defenses without the illness.
The childhood schedule is timed so protection arrives before a child is most at risk from each disease.
High vaccination rates also protect those who can't be vaccinated, through community (herd) immunity.
Mild, short-lived reactions like a sore arm or low fever are common; serious reactions are rare.
content_html: A vaccine is essentially a training exercise for the immune system. It presents a harmless piece of a germ — or a weakened version of it — so the body learns to recognize and fight that disease, without the child ever having to suffer the illness to gain the protection.
extra_html: The childhood immunization schedule isn't arbitrary: it's timed so that protection is in place before a child is most vulnerable to each disease. There's a community benefit too. When enough people are vaccinated, a disease has trouble spreading at all, which shields those who can't be vaccinated — newborns, or people with certain medical conditions — through what's called herd immunity. Mild reactions like a sore arm or a low fever are common and short-lived; serious reactions are rare. The exact schedule and any questions about your child are best handled by your pediatrician. This is general educational information.

related.title: Fever Basics for Parents
related.hook: A fever is a sign the body is fighting infection, not a disease itself — how your child looks and acts often matters more than the exact number on the thermometer.

flashcards.prompt: How does a vaccine protect a child?

choices.text: It trains the immune system to recognize a germ before real exposure
It kills germs already causing an active illness
It replaces the need for the immune system entirely

flashcards.explanation_html: A vaccine presents a harmless or weakened piece of a germ so the immune system builds defenses in advance — without the child getting the disease.

flashcards.back_html: When enough people are vaccinated, a disease struggles to spread — protecting those who can't be vaccinated, like newborns or some patients.

flashcards.prompt: What kind of reaction to a vaccine is most common?

choices.text: Mild and short-lived, like a sore arm or low fever
Severe and long-lasting in most children

flashcards.explanation_html: Mild, brief reactions are common and expected as the immune system responds. Serious reactions are rare.
